title: Power of Attorney for Property Sales and Title Transfer 2026: Risks
desc: Power of attorney to sell or transfer property under the Civil Code: scope, term, when it ends, risks of buying on a power of attorney and tax obligations.
summary: The rules on powers of attorney when selling or transferring property: term, scope, cases in which it ends, and the risks of using a power of attorney instead of a sale contract.
body: p

Owners who live far away, abroad or are elderly often authorise a relative to sell or transfer their property. Some buyers also receive only a "full power of attorney" instead of a sale contract. This article summarises the rules of the Civil Code 2015 and common risks.
h2
1. What is a power of attorney contract?
p

Under Article 562, the authorised person performs the task in the name of the principal; remuneration is paid only if agreed. A transaction made by the representative within the scope creates rights and obligations for the principal (Article 139). In other words, a power of attorney does not transfer ownership: the property remains in the principal's name.
h2
2. Scope and term
ul
The authorised person may act only within the scope stated in the document and must notify that scope to the other party to the transaction (Article 141).
The term is agreed by the parties; if not agreed, the power of attorney is valid for 1 year from the date it is established (Article 563).
Sub-authorisation is allowed only with the principal's consent or in force majeure; it may not exceed the original scope, and the form must match the original authorisation (Article 564).
h2
3. When does a power of attorney end?
p

Under Clause 3, Article 140, representation by authorisation ends when: agreed; the term expires; the task is completed; a party unilaterally terminates; the principal or the authorised person dies; and on some other grounds.
p

The principal has the right to terminate unilaterally at any time (if paid, remuneration for work done must be paid plus compensation; if unpaid, reasonable advance notice is given), and must notify third parties in writing (Clause 1, Article 569).
h2
4. Risks of "buying a house on a power of attorney"
ul

The buyer is not named on the property; if the seller (principal) dies or unilaterally terminates the authorisation, the authorisation ends (Clause 3, Article 140), while the property is still in the seller's name.
A transaction made as a sham to conceal another transaction is void as to the sham transaction (Article 124); in a dispute, the buyer must prove payment was made.

If the authorised person acts beyond the scope or has no power of representation, that part of the transaction does not bind the principal, unless the principal agrees or knew and did not object (Article 142, Article 143).
p
To buy property safely, sign a notarised or certified sale or transfer contract and then register the title transfer – see Notarising Property Sale Contracts 2026.
h2
5. Notarising a power of attorney
ul
An authorisation document concerning rights over real estate with no limitation must be notarised in the province where the property is located (Article 44 of the Notarisation Law).

Where the two parties are in different places: the principal has it notarised at a place of their choice, and the authorised person has it further notarised on the original at another place (Article 57).
h2
6. A "full power" authorisation is still taxed
p

An authorisation in which the recipient has the full content of ownership rights over the real estate is treated as a real estate transfer and is subject to 2% personal income tax; the taxpayer is the individual who gave the authorisation (Article 11 and Point b, Clause 6, Article 57 of Decree 253/2026/ND-CP). See Personal Income Tax on Property Sales 2026.
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The Notarisation Law 2024 has had some articles amended by Law No. 106/2025/QH15 (not yet in our library) and will be amended further from 1 January 2027. Before signing a power of attorney involving property, ask a notary or lawyer.
